"Northern Territory police failed to act on a string of self-harm and suicide attempts in caged police vehicles before the death of a vulnerable 23-year-old man last year, a coroner has found. NT coroner Greg Cavanagh has criticised police for failing to act on an internal report recommending CCTV cameras be installed in caged vehicles in 2013, following an earlier death in custody. In the three years between the two deaths, there were at least 16 attempted suicides in caged vehicles. “In six cases the persons were not detected until they were semi-conscious or unconscious,” Cavanagh found. “It wasn’t a matter of if a person would die in the back of a police van but when.”

On 16 September last year, two officers were making their way through Darwin, on their way to investigate a noise complaint, when they came across the scene of a serious crash. A Toyota Hilux had smashed into a palm tree on the corner of the Stuart Highway and Bargot Road, not far from Darwin airport. Hiding behind some vegetation was Dale Scott Walkinshaw, 23. Walkinshaw was unharmed but held his passenger in his arms. The young woman, whom he had met earlier at a bar, was in and out of consciousness, having suffered an injury to her back. Walkinshaw was well over the limit, returning a reading of 0.149.

Police quickly arrested Walkinshaw for dangerous driving due to intoxication. He was placed in the caged rear compartment of a patrol vehicle without restraints, despite his visibly distressed mental state. Officers later reported he was “quiet and withdrawn” but did not appear to be an immediate threat to himself or others.

Unseen by officers, shortly after departure, Walkinshaw attempted to take his own life using a ligature made from his clothing. Despite being within earshot, the officers did not notice the signs of distress. By the time he was discovered—slumped and unresponsive—medical intervention was too late. He was declared dead upon arrival at Royal Darwin Hospital.

The tragic incident prompted an extensive inquest, during which it was revealed that multiple red flags had been ignored for years. The 2013 internal police report, sparked by the death of another detainee in a police van, had urged the installation of real-time video monitoring and enhanced welfare checks. Yet, despite budget allocations and repeated recommendations, no action was taken.

Coroner Cavanagh delivered a damning conclusion: systemic failures, lack of accountability, and indifference to mental health risks had led to an entirely preventable death. “The signs were there. The warnings were clear. This was not misfortune—it was negligence,” he stated.

In the aftermath, the Northern Territory government announced an urgent review of custodial transport protocols, including the immediate rollout of CCTV in all police vehicles and mandatory mental health training for frontline officers. Walkinshaw’s family, advocating for justice and reform, have called for a royal commission into deaths in custody, highlighting the disproportionate impact on Indigenous Australians and the vulnerable.

Dale’s death has become a rallying cry for change—an emblem of what can happen when oversight is ignored, and lives are treated as afterthoughts. As Cavanagh wrote in his final remarks: “We must not wait for another grave to act. These are people, not statistics.”"
